ccpa/cross-border-transfer.obligation: No restriction on cross-border transfers of personal information.
ccpa/cross-border-transfer.verdict: Every specific term was absent across all 27 ingested sections: no adequacy concept, no contractual-safeguard mechanism, no 'cross-border', no 'outside the territory'. The one provision reached by a broad term is §1798.199, which lets the Agency cooperate with privacy authorities in other states and countries — regulator coordination, not a restriction on transfers. The statute governs what a business may do with personal information and says nothing about geography.

gdpr/data-localization.verdict: Chapter V controls export, not location. A transfer to a third country needs an adequacy decision (Art. 45) or appropriate safeguards (Art. 46), and Art. 44 makes those conditions general. None of them requires personal data to be stored in the Union, and Art. 1 points the other way: the Regulation's stated object includes the free movement of personal data. Reading an export restriction as a storage requirement is the common error, and it is the one this cell records as absent.

pdpo/data-localization.verdict: The nearest provision is not in force. Section 33 would prohibit transferring personal data 'to a place outside Hong Kong except in specified circumstances', and the ingested text carries its status in the heading: '(Not yet in operation)'. It was enacted in 1995 and has never been commenced. Even commenced it would restrict export rather than require local storage — and DPP4(2) runs the other way, expressly contemplating 'a data processor, whether within or outside Hong Kong'. So this cell is 0 twice over: the provision would not localise, and it does not apply.

pdpo/dpia.verdict: None of the six terms appears in the Ordinance: no 'impact assessment', no 'privacy impact', no 'prior consultation', no 'high risk'. No provision requires an assessment before a new or higher-risk use of personal data.
pdpo/dpia.elsewhere: The strictness 1 rests on PCPD guidance encouraging privacy impact assessments.

pdpo/dpo-representative.obligation: Appointing a data protection officer is recommended best practice, not a legal requirement.
pdpo/dpo-representative.verdict: 'Data protection officer' and 'privacy officer' appear nowhere in the Ordinance, and no provision requires a data user to designate anyone responsible for compliance. The four provisions reached only by broad terms use 'representative' in an unrelated sense — 'bodies representative of data users', whom the Commissioner consults before issuing a code of practice.
pdpo/dpo-representative.elsewhere: The strictness 1 rests on the PCPD's best-practice guidance recommending a data protection officer. Appointing one is sound practice and is not required by the text.

pipeda/rights-automated-decision.verdict: Nothing to show, and that is the finding. Across 120 indexed provisions the Act does not contain the string 'automat' at all — nor 'profil', nor any of the seven terms searched. This is the strongest form of absence a trace can record: not a near-miss judged insufficient, but vocabulary that is simply not in the instrument.
pipeda/rights-automated-decision.elsewhere: Automated decision-making rules were proposed in Bill C-27, alongside AIDA; both lapsed on prorogation in January 2025. Sector regulators and the Québec regime address automated decisions where PIPEDA does not.

quebec-law25/data-localization.verdict: Section 17 is an export gate, not a localisation rule: before communicating personal information outside Québec an enterprise must conduct a privacy impact assessment, and may proceed only if the assessment establishes that the information 'would receive adequate protection'. That restricts sending data out under conditions; it does not require data to stay. Section 8 goes only to disclosure — the person concerned must be informed of the possibility that their information could be communicated outside Québec.
